extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, psychology, and inductive logic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the standards, methodological rules, and evaluative principles the chapter gives for treating the study of mind as a science (distinguishing empirical vs causal laws, methods of induction, and the role of physiology). Useful for assessing or constructing scientific work on human nature and mental phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness of a science
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is exact when 'its phenomena have been brought under laws comprehending the whole of the causes by which the phenomena are influenced, whether in a great or only in a trifling degree, whether in all or only in some cases, and assigning to each of those causes the share of effect which really belongs to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Astronomy became exact when perturbations were accounted for; to be exact a discipline must account for both main and minor causes and apportion effects to causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of approximate/empirical generalizations when minor causes unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: When minor causes are not sufficiently ascertained, combine 'the exact laws of the greater causes' with 'empirical laws or such approximate generalizations' to 'lay down general propositions which will be true in the main.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combined propositions are useful for expectation and conduct but require allowance for probable inaccuracy; explicitly state degree of probable inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive connection of empirical truths to universal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'indispensable that these approximate generalizations...should be connected deductively with the laws of nature from which they result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show the causal origins of empirical rules so as to 'show the proper limits of those approximate truths' and enable deduction of results for new circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct subject-matter: Laws of Mind vs Laws of Body
rubrics_metrics.description: All states of mind are produced either by other states of mind (laws of Mind) or directly by states of body (laws of Body).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify phenomena accordingly: sensations (proximate bodily antecedents) belong to physiology; other mental states may be laws of Mind and require distinct treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject of Psychology: uniformities of succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychology studies 'the uniformities of succession, the laws...according to which one mental state succeeds another; is caused by, or at least, is caused to follow, another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the sequences/co-occurrences of mental states and their regularities as the proper objects of psychological science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of direct observation and experiment for mental laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we are ignorant of the characteristics of nervous antecedents, 'our only mode of studying their successions or co-existences must be by observing the successions and co-existences of the mental states' themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer mental laws solely from physiology; use experimental and observational psychological methods to establish laws of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Association (three principal laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the laws of association: (1) similar ideas tend to excite one another; (2) when two impressions have been frequently experienced together or in immediate succession, recurrence of one tends to excite the other; (3) greater intensity is equivalent to greater frequency in rendering ideas excitable by one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as elementary, empirically ascertained principles that generate more complex mental regularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental chemistry / generation of complex ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When many impressions or ideas operate together they may 'melt and coalesce' into a Complex Idea which should be said to 'result from, or be generated by, the simple ideas' rather than strictly 'consist of' them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize both compositional and emergent (chemical-like) processes in producing complex mental phenomena; analyze when elements are consciously distinguishable vs fused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Method of Agreement then Method of Difference to establish causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that an associated group of ideas was present when a complex feeling appears 'amounts only to the Method of Agreement' which 'is not enough' and must be followed 'by the Method of Difference' to prove causation experimentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing that association generates a phenomenon (e.g., belief or moral reprobation), design experiments that test whether introducing the alleged cause produces the effect (difference test).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study generated phenomena independently even if reducible
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one class of mental phenomena can be shown to be generated from simpler ones, 'it no more supersedes the necessity of an experimental study of the generated phenomenon' itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct direct empirical study of complex phenomena (beliefs, desires, volitions) rather than relying solely on reduction to simpler constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for individual differences (three sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of susceptibility among minds 'may be, first, original and ultimate facts; or, secondly, ... consequences of the previous mental history of those individuals; or, thirdly and lastly, they may depend on varieties of physical organization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining variability, analyze contributions from innate disposition, past mental history (habit, education), and physiological organisation; do not attribute differences dogmatically to immutable 'character'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider indirect influence of organic differences via sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic differences may 'render the pleasurable sensation itself more intense...so that the idea of the pleasure will also be an intenser feeling, and will, by the operation of mere mental laws, excite an intenser desire' without direct influence on the desire itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model how bodily variation affects downstream mental states indirectly through altered sensations; avoid simplistic claims of direct causation without tracing mediating psychological processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical laws from causal (scientific) laws
rubrics_metrics.description: An Empirical Law 'is a uniformity...true in all instances within our limits of observation, but is not of a nature to afford any assurance that it would hold beyond those limits.' 'The really scientific truths...are the causal laws which explain' empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer explanations in terms of underlying causes; treat empirical generalizations as checks on theory and as provisional, not ultimate, truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in generalizing empirical laws beyond observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If we have not yet accounted for the empirical law—if it rests only on observation—there is no safety in applying it far beyond the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which the observations were made.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the limits (time/place/circumstance) when using empirical generalizations; seek causal account before extrapolating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mental phenomena for study
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental phenomena are classified as 'Thoughts, Emotions, Volitions, and Sensations; the last being as truly states of Mind as the three former.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to organize observation, experiment, and theoretical accounts in psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate physiological findings but not substitute them for psychological analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The relations...of that science to the science of physiology must never be overlooked...But, on the other hand, to reject the resource of psychological analysis, and construct the theory of the mind solely on such data as physiology at present affords, seems...an error.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine physiological insight with direct psychological methods; do not collapse mental laws into current physiological ignorance—use both domains complementarily.
